name: Forbidden City
info: The Forbidden City is the imperial palace complex in the centre of Beijing, built from 1406 to 1420 under the Yongle Emperor and home to 24 Ming and Qing emperors until 1924, now the Palace Museum.

facts.made: Built for the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty, who moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing; construction took 14 years and more than a million workers; altered by the Qing rulers
facts.form: A walled rectangle 961 m by 753 m with a moat, holding 980 surviving buildings with 8,886 bays of rooms, chiefly of wood on marble terraces, divided into an Outer Court and an Inner Court
facts.where: The centre of Beijing, administered by the Palace Museum; part of the former imperial collection is in the National Palace Museum in Taipei
facts.known: residence of 24 Ming and Qing emperors; the Hall of Supreme Harmony; yellow glazed roofs; the central north-south axis of Beijing; the Palace Museum's collections; a World Heritage Site since 1987

t: Built from 1406 to 1420, the palace was the ceremonial and political centre of the Chinese government for over 500 years.
Its layout, colours and numbers were planned to express imperial majesty and the order of heaven and earth.
Since 1925 it has been the Palace Museum, whose collections grew from the Ming and Qing imperial collections.
dyk: A common story says the palace has 9,999 rooms, but survey evidence counts 8,886 bays of rooms in 980 surviving buildings.
ev: Construction begins after the Yongle Emperor moves the capital from Nanjing to Beijing
The palace becomes the seat of the Ming dynasty
Li Zicheng captures the palace and sets fire to parts of it as he flees; the Qing proclaim the Shunzhi Emperor there
Anglo-French forces occupy the palace during the Second Opium War
The abdication of Puyi ends its role as the political centre of China
The Palace Museum is established after Puyi's eviction in 1924
Part of the evacuated collection is shipped to Taiwan under orders of Chiang Kai-shek
UNESCO declares it a World Heritage Site as the Imperial Palace of the Ming and Qing Dynasties

sections.origins:
When Zhu Di, a son of the Hongwu Emperor, became the Yongle Emperor of the Ming dynasty, he moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing, and construction of the new palace began in 1406. The palace was designed as the centre of the walled city of Beijing, enclosed within a larger walled Imperial City, which was itself enclosed by the Inner City, with the Outer City to the south.

The site carried older plans with it. The palace's central north-south axis became the central axis of Beijing, running south through Tiananmen Gate towards Yongdingmen and north through Jingshan Park to the Drum Tower and Bell Tower. The axis is tilted by slightly more than two degrees from true north, and researchers now believe it was laid out during the Yuan dynasty to align with Shangdu, the Yuan empire's other capital. The layout also followed ancient customs set down in the Book of Rites, with ancestral temples in front of the palace, storage in the front part of the complex and residences at the back. In the Ming and Qing dynasties the palace was also known as Danei, or the Palace City, and today it is most commonly called Gugong, the Former Palace.
sections.content:
The Forbidden City is a rectangle 961 metres from north to south and 753 metres from east to west, surrounded by a wall 7.9 metres high and a moat 52 metres wide, with a gate on each side and corner towers. It is divided into the Outer Court to the south, used for ceremonies, and the Inner Court to the north, where the emperor and his family lived and day-to-day affairs of state were handled. The most important buildings stand on the central axis along the Imperial Way, on which only the emperor could normally walk or ride.

In the Outer Court three halls stand on a three-tiered white marble terrace: the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the largest surviving wooden structure in China and the ceremonial centre of imperial power, the Hall of Central Harmony and the Hall of Preserving Harmony, where the final stage of the imperial examinations was held. The Inner Court has its own three halls, the residences of emperor and empress, standing for Yang and Yin, with the Six Western and Six Eastern Palaces of the consorts beside them, the Imperial Garden behind and the Qianlong Emperor's Palace of Tranquil Longevity to the north-east.
sections.making:
Construction lasted 14 years and required more than a million workers. The builders used whole logs of precious Phoebe zhennan wood from the jungles of south-western China and large blocks of marble from quarries near Beijing, and the floors of the major halls were paved with specially baked golden bricks from Suzhou. The walls have a rammed earth core faced on both sides with three layers of baked brick. The northern ceremonial ramp behind the Hall of Preserving Harmony is carved from one stone of some 200 tons, and such slabs were probably moved from the quarry on ice sledges along a path lubricated with well water.

The design was planned in detail to express philosophical and religious principles and the majesty of imperial power. Almost all roofs bear yellow glazed tiles, the emperor's colour, except the library, roofed in black for water and protection from fire, and the crown prince's residences, in green for growth. The main halls stand in threes, the shape of the trigram for Heaven, and the Inner Court residences in sixes, the trigram for Earth. The number of statuettes on a roof ridge marked a building's rank, and only the Hall of Supreme Harmony had ten.
sections.reception:
The palace took its name from its scale and from the strict ban on entry for all but the emperor, the imperial family and their eunuch servants; unauthorised entry was punished by immediate execution. Its Chinese name Zijincheng, first formally recorded in 1576, links it with the North Star, the heavenly home of the Jade Emperor, so that the earthly emperor's residence mirrored the celestial one. From 1420 to 1644 it was the seat of the Ming dynasty.

In April 1644 the rebel Li Zicheng captured it and proclaimed the Shun dynasty, then fled before Wu Sangui and the Manchus, setting fire to parts of the palace. The Qing proclaimed the Shunzhi Emperor there that October, renamed principal buildings to stress harmony rather than supremacy, made the nameplates bilingual in Chinese and Manchu and brought shamanist worship into the Palace of Earthly Tranquility; under the Qing the Hall of Supreme Harmony served only for ceremonies such as enthronements and imperial weddings. Taoist and Buddhist shrines also stood in the Inner Court. Qing emperors lived and worked almost entirely in the Inner Court, and from the Yongzheng Emperor's reign in the Hall of Mental Cultivation.
sections.survival:
Foreign troops occupied the palace twice: Anglo-French forces in 1860 during the Second Opium War, and the forces of the treaty powers in 1900 and the following year, after Empress Dowager Cixi fled during the Boxer Rebellion. Puyi's abdication in 1912 ended its role as China's political centre, though he stayed in the Inner Court until a coup evicted him in 1924, and the Palace Museum was founded there in 1925. From 1933 the threat of Japanese invasion forced the evacuation of its treasures; after the war part returned, but in 1948 the Nationalist government shipped a selection to Taiwan, where it became the core of the National Palace Museum in Taipei.

After 1949 some damage was done in revolutionary zeal, and there were several plans to demolish the complex or reuse the site. During the Cultural Revolution Premier Zhou Enlai sent an army battalion to guard it. It was on China's first list of national priority protected sites in 1961. In the early 21st century the Palace Museum carried out a sixteen-year restoration to return the buildings to their state before 1911, opening further areas such as the Shoukang and Cining palaces.
sections.legacy:
The Forbidden City has shaped the later development of Chinese architecture and influenced building in East Asia and beyond, and UNESCO, which listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1987, recognises it as the largest collection of preserved ancient wooden structures in the world. Its axis still organises Beijing, running south through Tiananmen Gate to Tiananmen Square, the ceremonial centre of the People's Republic of China, and development around it is controlled by a buffer zone set out in 2004.

The Palace Museum holds 1,862,690 works of art by its latest audit, among them 340,000 ceramics, close to 50,000 paintings, bronzes from the early Shang dynasty, some 30,000 jades and more than 1,000 mechanical timepieces of the 18th and 19th centuries; the Ming and Qing government documents of the imperial libraries are now in the First Historical Archives. The palace has been the setting of films, from The Forbidden City of 1918 to The Last Emperor of 1987, the first feature film the People's Republic authorised to be shot inside it, and a large replica at Hengdian World Studios serves film-makers. Many Chinese see it as a cultural link to their ancestors.

summary: The Forbidden City in Beijing was built from 1406 to 1420 and served as the palace and seat of government of 24 Ming and Qing emperors until 1924. Planned to express imperial order in its layout and symbols, it survived fire, occupation and revolution and has been the Palace Museum since 1925.
